agentCan: Register public clients programmatically via Dynamic Client Registration and implement the full flow
Implement single-use refresh handling with atomic token persistence

approval.trigger: No review of OAuth applications is described anywhere in the OAuth documentation. Registration (manual or dynamic) is self-serve, and users can authorize the app once it exists: no submission step, no approval queue, no stated waiting period, no user cap before approval, and no cost in the docs read. (An absence-of-review finding: the docs simply contain no review step for OAuth apps.) The DigitalOcean Marketplace 'Add-Ons' program is separate; nothing in the OAuth docs ties OAuth apps to a Marketplace listing or review.

blockers.detail: 'You can use a refresh token exactly once to create a new access token (and refresh token). Doing so invalidates the access token that the refresh token was issued with.' You must persist the new refresh token on every refresh; losing it, or racing two refreshes, breaks the connection.
blockers.howToClear: Persist the replacement token pair atomically and serialize refreshes per connection.
blockers.title: Single-use refresh tokens that kill the old access token

blockers.detail: Two scope layers exist: legacy broad scopes (read; read write) and granular custom scopes (<resource>:<action>, e.g. droplet:create, database:read), plus aliases api:read (all read scopes) and api:write (equivalent to all scopes). The aliases 'automatically expand to include new API endpoints as they are added', so an api:write grant silently grows over time. And if you omit the scope parameter, the consent screen shows a 'Manage permissions' option letting the USER select specific granular scopes: your app may receive less than it assumed.
blockers.howToClear: Request explicit granular scopes rather than aliases or omission, and read the granted scope from the token response.
blockers.title: Alias scopes expand silently; omitting scope hands the choice to the user

alternatives: Public client (native, desktop, CLI, and explicitly MCP clients): no secret, PKCE S256 only, typically created via Dynamic Client Registration; 1-hour access tokens
flavor.recommended: A confidential OAuth application registered manually in the control panel (OAuth Applications page), authorization code flow
flavor.why: The OAuth API 'lets you obtain limited access to DigitalOcean teams': tokens are granted against a team, and the token response carries the user's and team's UUIDs/names. Confidential clients (server-side web apps that can hold a secret) get a client_id and client_secret from the control panel; the redirect_uri you send must 'match a callback URL you provided during application registration'.

humanMust: Register the confidential application in the control panel and custody the client_secret
For DCR clients: store the registration_access_token from the registration response (shown only there, never retrievable again)
name: DigitalOcean
nuances: DCR details: POST /v1/oauth/register accepts 1-5 redirect_uris; the server publishes a metadata document at cloud.digitalocean.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server so clients can discover endpoints and self-register programmatically. Deleting a dynamically registered client (DELETE /register/{client_id}) removes the client along with its tokens and grants.

Public-client redirects are flexible: loopback redirect URIs (127.0.0.1, [::1], localhost) match on any port, so native apps can use ephemeral ports. Confidential-client access tokens expire in 30 days (expires_in 2592000); public-client tokens in 1 hour (3600). Token prefixes: doo_v1_ (access), dor_v1_ (refresh).

prompt=none silent flow: already-authorized signed-in users are redirected back with a new token; others get error=consent_required or error=login_required. An account hint can be supplied via the first 6 characters of an expected account UUID.

Implicit-flow discrepancy: the /authorize documentation still describes response_type=token (implicit, token in the callback fragment) for client-side apps, while the published authorization-server metadata lists response_types_supported ['code'] only and grant_types_supported ['authorization_code', 'refresh_token']. The docs present both; plan on the code flow.
Tokens are team-scoped in effect: authorization grants access to a team, so multi-team users pick which team they are connecting.
prerequisites: A DigitalOcean account (control panel registration for confidential clients)
A callback URL provided at registration (runtime redirect_uri must match it)

steps.detail: Confidential: in the control panel, on the OAuth Applications page, register the application (this assigns the client ID and client secret, and records your callback URL). Public/MCP/CLI alternative: POST JSON to cloud.digitalocean.com/v1/oauth/register (redirect_uris 1-5, token_endpoint_auth_method 'none', grant_types including authorization_code) and store the returned registration_access_token, which is shown only in that response and required to read/update/delete the client later.
steps.title: Register the application

steps.detail: GET cloud.digitalocean.com/v1/oauth/authorize with client_id, redirect_uri, response_type=code, optional scope (omit it and the user picks granular scopes via 'Manage permissions'), state (recommended), prompt, and for public clients code_challenge + code_challenge_method=S256. The signed-in user authorizes the app for a team.
steps.title: Send the user to authorize

steps.detail: POST cloud.digitalocean.com/v1/oauth/token with grant_type=authorization_code, code, client_id, redirect_uri, and client_secret (confidential) or code_verifier (public). Response: access_token (doo_v1_), refresh_token (dor_v1_), expires_in (2592000 for confidential, 3600 for public), granted scope, and user/team info.
steps.title: Exchange the code

steps.detail: Call api.digitalocean.com/v2 with Authorization: Bearer. Refresh via POST /token with grant_type=refresh_token, remembering each refresh token is single-use and refreshing invalidates the prior access token; persist the new pair atomically. Revoke via POST /revoke.
steps.title: Call the API; handle single-use refresh

tagline: No review at all, and public clients (including MCP clients) can even register themselves programmatically. The sharp edges are in token behavior: refresh tokens are single-use and refreshing invalidates the old access token, and the convenient alias scopes quietly expand as the API grows.

time.active: ~5 min registration + ~1 hr of flow code
time.total: Same day; no review documented in front of users
